Ah @Akash-Kumar-Sen I realised there are two errors, one for MariaDB (https://djangoci.com/job/pr-mariadb/database=mysql,label=mariadb,python=python3.11/21757/console) this is failing on the table creation and the other failures are (as you said) for the test `delete.tests.DatabaseLevelOnDeleteTests.test_foreign_key_db_default`

I am reading the MySQL documentation on foreign keys here: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/create-table-foreign-keys.html
This sounds interesting:
> - SET DEFAULT: This action is recognized by the MySQL parser, but both [InnoDB](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-storage-engine.html) and [NDB](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/mysql-cluster.html) reject table definitions containing ON DELETE SET DEFAULT or ON UPDATE SET DEFAULT clauses.

> For storage engines that support foreign keys, MySQL rejects any [INSERT](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/insert.html) or [UPDATE](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/update.html) operation that attempts to create a foreign key value in a child table if there is no matching candidate key value in the parent table.

Apparently MariaDB uses the InnoDB storage engine by default - I think that explains why the table create is failing there. 

It makes me think _maybe_ Django should not allow `on_delete=DB_SET_DEFAULT` for MySQL :thinking:

The test I'd like to see would hit the actual database. 

Something like: 

1. Create a pair of models with `CASCADE`. 
2. Create some instances. 
3. Delete the parent model. 
4. Assert the children were deleted (by Django)
5. Migrate the child model to use `DB_CASCADE`. 
6. Create some more instances. 
7. Delete the parent model again. 
8. Assert the children were deleted (by the database). 

It's step 8 that failed for me (because the field was never updated).

It's possible to have database cascade deletion in Django globally, using a custom "engine". For example, for PostgreSQL, we can put this into `custom_postgresql/base.py`:

```py
from django.db import models
from django.db.backends.postgresql import base


class DatabaseSchemaEditor(base.DatabaseSchemaEditor):
    sql_create_column_inline_fk = None

    def _create_fk_sql(self, model, field, suffix):
        statement = super()._create_fk_sql(model, field, suffix)
        if field.remote_field.on_delete is models.deletion.CASCADE:
            statement.template = statement.template.replace('%(deferrable)s', ' ON DELETE CASCADE' + '%(deferrable)s')
        return statement


class DatabaseWrapper(base.DatabaseWrapper):
    SchemaEditorClass = DatabaseSchemaEditor
```

and reference `custom_postgresql` as `ENGINE` in `DATABASES`. This can be easily extended to support other deletion actions (`RESTRICT`, `SET NULL`, `SET DEFAULT`).

Additionally, for performance, `can_fast_delete` should return `True` most of the time, to disable Django's default behaviour:

```py
models.deletion.Collector.can_fast_delete = lambda self, objs, *args, **kwargs: hasattr(objs, '_meta') or hasattr(objs, '_raw_delete')
```

This works for all models and foreign key fields (including M2M) automatically. If you want to use it in an existing application, you need to recreate the existing constraints first (by setting `db_constraint=False` everywhere, generating a migration, reverting the change, and generating a migration again).

---

Since this pull request seems to not be moving forward, is there a reason the above simpler solution couldn't be built into Django instead?

> Since this pull request seems to not be moving forward, is there a reason the above simpler solution couldn't be built into Django instead?

There are few ones yes, I would invite you to read the full discussions here and on [the decade old ticket](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/21961).

One example is that your solution completely breaks signals and `delete`/`save` method overrides which might be an acceptable compromise for your project but not something we can silently enable given the impact it would have on third-party applications as well as first party one which have overridden these methods with business logic that would now be silently circumvented.

Of course no-one suggests changing the logic "silently". It could be an opt-in feature, as a global setting. Signals and method overrides have many documented gotchas already, like [`QuerySet.delete`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/models/querysets/#delete) and [`QuerySet.update`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/models/querysets/#update), so this would be no different. Anyway, I'll keep maintaining the workaround then.
